prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and thereby showing how reallocation across firms shapes who exports and invests abroad and how countries gain from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 as the sole part, credited to Helpman and Melitz. What changed is the wording and the ordering of my alternatives, as explained below. The case rests on content. Melitz (2003) and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) moved trade analysis from industries and representative firms to firms that differ in productivity and select into exporting and foreign investment. This identified reallocation across firms as a distinct channel for the gains from trade and opened a firm-level empirical agenda. The predictions have been confronted with firm microdata in many countries for more than twenty years, and where the baseline failed in detail the framework was extended rather than abandoned. As an economic historian I value work that changes what we measure and how we understand what we measure, and this did both. The exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. Hassler and Strömberg moved from B006 first to B001 first on discovery boundary and attribution, and I find those stated reasons substantive, though I treat the movement and the count of eleven first places as no evidence of merit. The chair rightly warns that convergence among files from one model may reflect shared reasoning patterns, so I tested the strongest objections below instead of relying on the tally. The attribution to the pair is defensible on the record. Melitz supplies the canonical selection model, and Helpman supplies the exports-versus-FDI sorting result and the earlier differentiated-product foundations. I propose a single part because B001 already uses two of the three permitted names. No other shortlisted achievement fits the remaining slot without fragmenting its credit: B006 with Pakes alone would split the BLP core, and B034 requires two names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions, including the exporter-premia facts and the Eaton-Kortum framework, and none is credited on this ballot entry. If the Committee judges the discovery to be the whole firm-level trade programme, with theory, facts and quantification, then a two-name award is too narrow and the ballot cannot repair that. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is also excluded, and I have flagged that my own thematic interest in spatial growth could bias me toward giving it more weight. Separately, the baseline model's sharper predictions are rejected in detail and its welfare implications depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions. A citation that implied settled welfare magnitudes would overclaim. The earlier trade prize in 2008 also leaves a question of incremental novelty for the lineage. I read selection across heterogeneous firms as a distinct step from scale economies and product differentiation with representative firms, but that is a judgment and not a fact the record settles. Finally, B001 is theory-led, and its link to policy practice is more indirect than B006's direct use in antitrust and merger review.

responses.point: Boppart treats the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as a real attribution risk. He keeps B034 as a serious alternative only if the overlap with the 2022 prize is judged not disqualifying, and he sees the empirical identification of the collateral channel as less direct than the theory.
responses.response: I agree that the omission is the largest risk to B001, and I do not want to resolve it by assertion. My position after this round is that the committee may credit only the names on the entry. The empirical precursors can be acknowledged in the scientific background, and the citation should name selection and reallocation and not claim the exporter-premia facts or the Eaton-Kortum line. This only works if the Committee accepts that the discovery is the model that organised those facts and generated the new welfare channel. I stated in round 1 that this is a judgment about the discovery's boundary, and I still hold that. On B034 your point about indirect identification has moved me. It is a reason I now place B034 behind B006 among my alternatives, even though its two-name attribution is cleaner than most.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B006 first to B001 first, citing a tighter discovery boundary and cleaner credit. He concedes that B001 is theory-led with an indirect link to policy compared with B006's direct use in antitrust and merger review, and he keeps B006 as the first alternative.
responses.response: I accept the policy-reach point. Merger review is a more direct channel than trade-liberalisation evaluation, and I have reordered my alternatives to put B006 first because of it. I would resist letting it decide the matter, since reach in policy practice and a change in what a field theorises are different virtues. On the chair's boundary question for B006, I think a defensible prize would have to be limited to demand estimation (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes), with the dynamic-games strand and the Bresnahan and Reiss lineage acknowledged but not credited. That is a narrower claim than the ballot's seven names, and I can support it only in that form. It is also why I do not propose B006 as a co-equal second part.

responses.point: Strömberg supports the two-name B001 configuration but says that calling Redding derivative understates his work. He says the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line cannot be dismissed easily, so the award is vulnerable if the Committee wants to cover the full firm-level lineage. He also says the baseline Melitz model's sharp predictions are rejected in detail.
responses.response: I agree with your correction on Redding. The case for omitting him is that his quantitative and spatial work extends the selection framework and is a separate achievement, not that it is minor. I also accept that the two-name award is exposed if the Committee frames the discovery broadly. This is the condition that would move me. If a majority holds that the achievement is the whole firm-level and quantitative trade programme, I would regard the B001 pair as too narrow, and I would rather move to B006's demand-estimation core than stretch B001 with names the ballot does not support. On your rejection point, I now put the limit directly into the citation. It speaks of reallocation shaping the gains from trade and does not state a welfare magnitude.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson argues that B006 bundles demand estimation, dynamic games and production-function strands, so its discovery boundary is fuzzy. She also says the B001 attribution to Melitz and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple is the more defensible, and that the citation must not overclaim the whole field.
responses.response: I agree on the boundary and on the wording, and the final citation reflects this. I would add one test I did not apply in round 1. A discovery boundary should be judged by whether a single sentence can state what is credited without a hidden list of exceptions. For B001 the sentence is selection of heterogeneous firms into exporting and investment, and the reallocation channel that follows. For B006 the equivalent sentence works only after the Committee has made a choice that the ballot entry itself does not make. That does not make B006 weak, and I still rank it as my first fallback. It does mean the Committee would have to settle the boundary before it votes.

responses.point: Krusell treats B034 as a clean Kiyotaki-Moore attribution and keeps it as his second choice. He regards the Gertler and Gilchrist extension as overlapping with the 2022 prize and sees the Melitz framework as a workhorse well beyond trade.
responses.response: We agree that the attribution of B034 is clean. In round 1 I argued that the overlap with 2022 cuts both ways, and I still think a citation tied specifically to the dynamic collateral-constraint mechanism would be distinguishable. Boppart's point on indirect identification, together with the fact that the empirical record is thinner than for B001, makes me keep B034 as an alternative and not a rival. On your point about use beyond trade, I agree, but I give it limited weight on its own. A framework can be widely borrowed without that settling who originated it, so I rest the case on the selection result and its tests in firm data.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee frames the discovery as the selection and reallocation framework (Helpman and Melitz) or as the wider firm-level and quantitative trade programme. This is the single judgment that would most change my position, and I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence.

Whether the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited on this ballot entry, can be handled by the citation and the scientific background or makes a two-name award too narrow.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial work should be credited as part of this achievement. I currently judge it a separate, later strand, and I note my thematic interest may bias me.
How far the sensitivity of the baseline model's welfare implications to distributional assumptions should limit the citation. I have worded it to avoid claiming magnitudes.

Whether B006 can be bounded to the demand-estimation core without arbitrary exclusion of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin, and how much weight methodological reach deserves against conceptual change.
My assessment rests on the round-1 files, the chair summary and general knowledge. I have not independently verified citation counts, priority records or award histories.
statement.conflict_note: No collaboration, supervision or institutional tie to Helpman, Melitz or any other credited name on the shortlist is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose thematic proximity only: my work on regional and spatial growth makes me more attentive to Redding's quantitative-spatial contributions, and I tested that against my view of B001. My co-author Johannes Lindvall is not a candidate. Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague on the committee and is not a candidate, and I disclose that tie without adjudicating it. No new conflict arose in the exchange.
